doc.title: Jane Ira Bloom interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 3, 1998

title: Commissioned by NASA
summary: Her letter to NASA led to the first music commission for the art program, a piece at Kennedy Space Center, and the STS 26 launch.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: Right. Well you seem to have pretty wide ranging tastes. And you were the first person commissioned by NASA to write. How did that come about?

I wrote a letter to NASA in the early 80s. I was just fascinated with whether NASA had ever thought about the future of the arts in space. I was very interested in what zero gravity might mean to the future of artistic performance. You know if there wasn’t gravity, how might music and dance and sculpture and theater, how all these things might be different. So I wondered whether NASA might have ever thought about it too. I wrote them a letter and six months later I got an envelope back from a gentleman named Robert Schulman, who is head of the NASA art program. I didn’t even know that this existed. And he was an avid jazz fan to boot. And I corresponded with him for years. And eventually our correspondence came up with the idea of how about commissioning the first musician instead of a visual artist to be part of this NASA art program. Basically they would invite you down with special access to go see a launch, a landing, and to tour

the various NASA facilities, to see things people never get to see. And it was an extraordinary experience. And from that experience you contribute a work of art to their traveling space art collection. And I wound up composing a piece for chamber orchestra and jazz musicians that got performed at the Kennedy Space Center in 1989, and involved six jazz musicians inside the orchestra, it involved live electronics that I used, and a sound surround speaker system. So it had all kinds of interesting new elements to it. It kind of foreshadowed work that I did later on in my own work.
Oh it was probably one of the highlights of my life, definitely.
What launch did you see by the way?

STS 26, which was the first return to flight launch after the Challenger accident. It was an exciting time, yeah. I got to meet a lot of interesting astronauts, I met astronaut John Young, shook hands with a man who had stepped on the moon. He actually spoke and gave a beautiful speech about the future of the arts and music in space, before we did the concert. It was quite wonderful.
